title: Same four rings, new stacks
stem: The same four rings are placed through a wooden stand, one on top of the other. Which one of the following is not a possible observation?

options.pick: Magnet 2 floats above a non-magnetic ring, not above a magnet, so it looks as if nothing is pushing it.
options.why: Magnet 1 pushes magnet 2 up through the non-magnetic ring when like poles face each other. The non-magnetic ring just rests on magnet 1, and the magnetic material sticks to the top of magnet 2. This is possible.

options.pick: The non-magnetic ring is high up on a floating magnet, and a magnet does not push or pull a non-magnetic ring.
options.why: The non-magnetic ring needs no magnetic force to stay there. It rests on magnet 1, the way a book rests on a table. Magnet 1 floats because magnet 2 pushes it. This is possible.

options.pick: Two magnets touching looks wrong if you think magnets always push each other away.
options.why: When unlike poles face each other, two magnets attract and stay together. The magnetic material sticks on top of magnet 1. This is possible.

title: A plastic ring in between
stem: Magnet P rests on a wooden stand. A plastic ring is placed on top of P. Magnet Q is then put on the stand, with its N pole facing the N pole of P. What will happen to Q?

options.text: Q rests on the plastic ring, because the plastic ring stops P from pushing Q.
options.pick: The plastic ring sits between the magnets, so it seems to block them.
options.why: A magnet can push through non-magnetic materials such as plastic. The plastic ring does not stop P pushing Q.

options.text: Q floats above the plastic ring, because P pushes Q away through the plastic.
options.pick: Check which poles face each other, then remember that plastic does not stop a magnet’s push.
options.why: N faces N, and like poles repel. P pushes Q away through the plastic ring, so Q floats above it.

options.text: Q floats above the plastic ring, because the plastic ring pushes Q away.
options.pick: Q is touching nothing but air above the plastic ring, so the ring seems to be doing the pushing.
options.why: Plastic is a non-magnetic material. A magnet neither pushes nor pulls it, and it cannot push a magnet. The push comes from P.

options.text: Q is pulled down onto the plastic ring, because P attracts Q.
options.pick: Two magnets close together are often seen sticking together.
options.why: Two magnets attract only when unlike poles face each other. Here N faces N: like poles, so they repel.

title: Reading Sam’s results
stem: Sam put magnet X on a wooden stand and placed a ring on top of it. Then he put magnet Y on the stand, with like poles of X and Y facing each other. He changed only the material of the ring each time and recorded whether Y floated. Which conclusion is correct?
figure:
Material of the ringDid Y float above the ring?
woodyes
plasticyes
glassyes
steelno

options.text: X’s push on Y acts through wood, plastic and glass.
options.pick: Read the three “yes” rows: Y floated with each of these rings in between.
options.why: Wood, plastic and glass are non-magnetic. Y still floated, so X pushed Y through each of them.

options.text: X can push Y only when nothing is placed between X and Y.
options.pick: It feels as if a magnet needs a clear space to push.
options.why: Y floated with a wood, plastic or glass ring in between, so X pushed Y through them. The table does not support this.

options.text: Y did not float on the steel ring because steel is a non-magnetic material.
options.pick: Something stopped Y floating, and “non-magnetic” sounds like the reason.
options.why: Steel is a magnetic material. Magnet Y attracts the steel ring and is pulled down onto it, so Y cannot float.

options.text: The wood, plastic and glass rings pushed Y up.
options.pick: Y floated just above these rings, so they seem to do the pushing.
options.why: Wood, plastic and glass are non-magnetic. They do not push or pull a magnet. Magnet X did the pushing.

title: Making it a fair test
stem: Sam wants to find out whether magnet X can push magnet Y through rings made of different materials. He places a ring between X and Y on a wooden stand and checks whether Y floats. To make it a fair test, what must he keep the same each time?

options.text: The material of the ring
options.pick: The material is the most important thing in the investigation, so it feels like it should be kept the same.
options.why: The material of the ring is what Sam is testing. It is the one thing he changes.

options.text: Whether Y floats
options.pick: Whether Y floats is mentioned in the investigation, so it seems to be something to control.
options.why: Whether Y floats is the result Sam observes. He cannot choose it; he finds it out.

options.text: Magnets X and Y, the poles that face each other, and the thickness of the ring
options.pick: List everything except the material that could change whether Y floats.
options.why: Only the material of the ring is changed. The magnets, the poles facing each other and the ring’s thickness could all affect the result, so they are kept the same.

options.text: Nothing else. Only the material is being tested, so the poles facing each other can change.
options.pick: Since only the material is being tested, the other things seem not to matter.
options.why: If unlike poles faced each other, Y would be pulled down whatever the ring was. Changing the poles would spoil the test, so they must stay the same.

options.pick: Magnet 2 floated before, so it seems it will float again.
options.why: Two magnets repel only when like poles face each other. Turning magnet 2 over brings its other pole to face magnet 1.

options.text: Nothing changes, because turning a magnet over does not change the pole that faces magnet 1.
options.pick: It is the same magnet, so it seems it should act the same way.
options.why: A magnet has two different poles, one at each end. Turning it over puts the opposite pole at the bottom.

options.text: The magnetic material ring is pushed off magnet 2, because a different pole of magnet 2 is now on top.
options.pick: A different pole on top seems to change how the magnetic material reacts.
options.why: Both poles of a magnet attract a magnetic material. The ring stays stuck to magnet 2.

options.text: Magnet 2 drops onto magnet 1 and they stay together, with the magnetic material ring still on top.
options.pick: Work out which pole of magnet 2 faces magnet 1 after turning it over.
options.why: Like poles faced each other before, so they repelled. After turning, unlike poles face each other, so they attract and magnet 2 drops onto magnet 1. The magnetic material is still attracted to magnet 2.

title: A paper clip on a wooden table
stem: A steel paper clip lies on top of a thin wooden table. Lin holds a magnet under the table, right below the paper clip, and slowly moves the magnet along. What happens to the paper clip?

options.text: It stays where it is, because the wooden table stops the magnet’s pull.
options.pick: The table is between the magnet and the paper clip, so it seems to block the pull.
options.why: Wood is a non-magnetic material. A magnet can pull through it, so the paper clip is still pulled.

options.text: It moves along with the magnet, because the magnet pulls it through the wood.
options.pick: Ask whether wood stops a magnet’s pull, and what steel is.
options.why: Steel is a magnetic material, so the magnet attracts it. The pull acts through the wood, so the paper clip follows the magnet.

options.text: It moves away from the magnet, because the magnet pushes steel away.
options.pick: Magnets push as well as pull, so the paper clip might be pushed.
options.why: A magnet only ever pulls a magnetic material such as steel. Only another magnet can be pushed away.

options.text: It moves, because the magnet pulls the wooden table and the table drags the paper clip.
options.pick: The table is the thing the magnet is touching, so it seems to be pulled.
options.why: Wood is non-magnetic, so the magnet does not pull the table. The magnet pulls the paper clip directly, through the wood.

title: Taking the plastic ring out
stem: Ring magnets A and B are on a wooden stand, with a plastic ring resting on A. B floats above the plastic ring. The plastic ring is taken out, and B is put back on the stand the same way round. What happens to B?

options.text: B falls onto A, because the plastic ring was what held B up.
options.pick: B was floating just above the plastic ring, so the ring seems to be holding it up.
options.why: Plastic is non-magnetic and does not push a magnet. A was pushing B all along, so B still floats.

options.text: B is pulled down onto A, because the poles facing each other are now different.
options.pick: Taking something away feels as if it should change the result.
options.why: B was put back the same way round, so the same like poles still face each other, and like poles repel.

options.text: B still floats above A, because A still pushes B away.
options.pick: Ask what was really holding B up: the plastic ring, or magnet A?
options.why: Like poles of A and B face each other, so A pushes B away. The plastic ring never stopped this push, so B still floats.

options.text: B floats higher than before, because the plastic ring was weakening A’s push.
options.pick: Something in between seems as if it must get in the way of the push.
options.why: Plastic does not stop or weaken a magnet’s push. B floats at the same height as before.

title: What is ring X?
stem: Ring X is stuck to the bottom of magnet K. K and X are put on a wooden stand above magnet L. K and X float, with a gap between X and L. What can X be?

options.text: A magnet
options.pick: X is the ring right above the gap. Ask what kind of object can be pushed away by L.
options.why: Only a magnet can be pushed away by another magnet. X sticks to K because unlike poles meet, and its other pole faces a like pole of L, so L pushes it up.

options.text: A steel ring that is not a magnet
options.pick: Steel sticks to K, and it seems K’s push could carry it up.
options.why: Magnet L would pull a steel ring across the gap, because a magnetic material is only ever pulled. There could be no gap.

options.text: A plastic ring
options.pick: A magnet’s push acts through plastic, so a plastic ring seems fine.
options.why: A plastic ring cannot stick to K, because a magnet does not pull plastic. It would drop onto L.

options.text: Either a magnet or a steel ring
options.pick: Both stick to magnet K, so both seem possible.
options.why: A steel ring right above the gap would be pulled down by L. Only a magnet works.
